questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
People expect the train to arrive on time.

options.text: It will expected that the train will arrive on time.
People are expected the train will arrive on time.
The train is expected to arrive on time.
The train was expected on time by people.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The train is expected to arrive on time.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The provided sentence is in the **Active Voice** and follows the standard syntax: **Subject** (People) + **Verb** (expect) + **Object** (the train) + **Infinitive Phrase** (to arrive on time).

• In the transition to **Passive Voice**, the **Object** of the active sentence (**the train**) must function as the **New Subject** of the passive sentence.

• The main verb **expect** is in the **Simple Present Tense**. According to English transformational grammar, the passive form for the simple present is **is/am/are + Past Participle (V3)**. Since **the train** is a **singular noun**, the auxiliary verb **is** is paired with the past participle **expected**.

• The **to-infinitive** (to arrive) remains in its active infinitive form because the expectation concerns the future action of the train itself. This is a common structure for verbs of **perception**, **calculation**, or **expectation**.

• The original subject **People** is a **General Agent**. In passive constructions, indefinite or general agents like **people**, **someone**, or **they** are typically omitted as the focus is placed entirely on the **action** or the **recipient**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Passive Voice**:

• The **Passive Voice** is used to emphasize the **action** (the expectation) and the **object** (the train) rather than the **subject** performing the action.

• It is widely utilized in **formal reporting**, **scientific writing**, and **news headlines** to maintain an objective tone.

• **Verbs of Opinion and Expectation**:

• Verbs such as **expect**, **believe**, **report**, **claim**, and **think** can be converted using two passive structures:

• **Personal Passive**: [Subject] + [Passive Verb] + [to-infinitive] (e.g., **The train is expected to arrive...**).

• **Impersonal Passive**: It + [Passive Verb] + [that-clause] (e.g., **It is expected that the train will arrive...**).

• **Tense Maintenance**:

• A fundamental rule of **voice conversion** is that the **tense** must remain constant. If the active verb is **Present Tense** (expect), the passive auxiliary must also be **Present** (is expected). Converting it to **was expected** (Past) or **will be expected** (Future) would fundamentally change the meaning of the original statement.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
Were the rare paintings being displayed by the gallery during the summer exhibition?

options.text: Did the gallery display the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?
Were the gallery displaying the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?
Was the gallery displaying the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?
Have the gallery displayed the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Was the gallery displaying the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The provided sentence 'Were the rare paintings being displayed by the gallery during the summer exhibition?' is in the **Passive Voice** of the **Past Continuous Tense** in an interrogative form.

• The structure for **Past Continuous (Passive Interrogative)** is: **Was/Were + Object + being + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Subject?**

• To convert this into the **Active Voice**, the structure must follow: **Was/Were + Subject + Verb-ing + Object?**

• In the passive sentence, **the rare paintings** is the object, and **the gallery** is the agent (subject). Hence, **the gallery** becomes the **grammatical subject** in the active voice.

• Since **the gallery** is a **singular collective noun** in this context, it requires the auxiliary verb **Was** rather than 'Were' to maintain subject-verb agreement.

• The passive construction **being displayed** is converted back to the active present participle form **displaying**.

• Combining these elements, the correct active construction is 'Was the gallery displaying the rare paintings during the summer exhibition?'.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Tense Conversion Rules**:

• **Simple Past**: Active (Did + Subject + V1) vs. Passive (Was/Were + Object + V3). Option 1 uses 'Did', which changes the **continuous aspect** of the original sentence.

• **Past Continuous**: Active (Was/Were + Subject + V1-ing) vs. Passive (Was/Were + Object + being + V3). This is the specific rule applicable here.

• **Present Perfect**: Active (Has/Have + Subject + V3) vs. Passive (Has/Have + Object + been + V3). Option 4 uses 'Have', which incorrectly changes the **tense** from past to present.

• **Subject-Verb Agreement**:

• In Option 2, the use of **Were** with **the gallery** is a grammatical error because a singular subject must be paired with a singular verb in standard **English grammar**.

</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The house smells ______ lichens.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**of**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** __ 
• The verb **smell** is typically followed by the preposition **of** when describing that something has a particular or characteristic scent. 
• The construction **smell of something** is used to indicate the source or the nature of the odor being emitted by the subject (**The house**). 
• In this context, the sentence indicates that the house emits the scent associated with **lichens**. 
• **Options 1, 2,** and **3** do not form the correct idiomatic or grammatical structure required to describe a specific scent in this sentence. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**. **Complete Sentence:** *'The house **smells of**__ lichens.'* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 
• **Smell of:** Used when something has a specific odor (e.g., **smells of garlic**, **smells of fresh rain**). 
• **Off:** In the context of smell, **off** is usually used as an adjective to mean food has gone bad (e.g., **the meat smells off**), but it is not used with an object like **lichens**. 
• **Smell like:** While **smell like** is also a common way to describe scents, **of** is the specific preposition provided in the correct grammatical context here. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The judge remarked that the arguments presented by the lawyer were devoid of logic and substance.

options.text: given by the lawyer were devoid in logic
told by the lawyer were devoid at logic
argued by the lawyer were devoid to logic

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**No improvement required**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence utilizes the **adjective phrase** **devoid of**, which is the standard **idiomatic expression** in the English language to signify that something is entirely **lacking** or free from a particular quality.
 
• Linguistically, the word **devoid** is derived from the Old French **desvuidier** (to empty), and in **modern English syntax**, it is exclusively paired with the preposition **of** to function as a **post-modifier** or within a **complementary phrase**.
 
• The verb **presented** is the most contextually appropriate **past participle** for a **courtroom setting**, as legal **arguments** are formally introduced, submitted, or **presented** by a **lawyer** to a **judge** for consideration.
 
• The **subject-verb agreement** is correctly maintained in the original sentence, where the **plural noun** **arguments** corresponds with the **plural verb** **were**.
 
• As the underlined portion **presented by the lawyer were devoid of logic** adheres to all rules of **syntax**, **collocation**, and **formal register**, no grammatical **improvement** is necessary.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prepositional Errors**:
 
 
• The use of **devoid in**, **devoid at**, or **devoid to** are common **grammatical errors**. In English, specific **adjectives** are bound to specific **prepositions** (fixed prepositions).
 
• Examples of correct **fixed prepositions** include **interested in**, **good at**, and **similar to**. Using any preposition other than **of** with **devoid** results in an **ungrammatical construction**.
 
 
 
• **Contextual Vocabulary**:
 
 
• **Logic and Substance**: In **legal discourse**, these terms refer to the **rational consistency** and the **factual weight** of an argument, respectively.
 
• **Legal Collocations**: While **told** or **given** are synonyms for communication, they lack the **professional nuance** required for **litigation**, where **arguments** are strictly **advanced** or **presented**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The executive committee is committed _________ bringing about a drastic change in the administration policy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**to**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The adjective **committed** is typically followed by the preposition **to** when expressing dedication or a pledge to a cause or action. 
• In the phrase **committed to**, the word **to** functions as a preposition, not as an infinitive marker. Therefore, it must be followed by a **noun** or a **gerund** (the -ing form of a verb). 
• In this sentence, **bringing** is the gerund form of the verb **bring**, which correctly follows the preposition **to**. 
• The other prepositions provided (**by**, **for**, **on**) do not idiomatically follow **committed** in this context. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**. **Complete Sentence:** *'The executive committee is **committed to**__ bringing about a drastic change in the administration policy.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• There are several other English expressions where **to** is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund rather than a base verb, such as: 
• **Look forward to** (e.g., I look forward to **meeting** you). 
• **Accustomed to** (e.g., She is accustomed to **waking** up early). 
• **Object to** (e.g., They object to **changing** the plan). 
• **Dedicated to** (e.g., He is dedicated to **improving** his skills). </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
The supervisor did not mind if a worker left early, provided he finishes his task for the day.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is **tense inconsistency**. The main clause 'The supervisor **did not mind**' and the subordinate clause 'if a worker **left** early' are both in the **Simple Past Tense**.
 
• The completion of the task is a condition that must have occurred **before** the worker left early. To describe an action that happened before another action in the past, the **Past Perfect Tense** is required.
 
• The Past Perfect Tense is formed using '**had + past participle**' (had finished).
 
• Therefore, '**finishes**' (Simple Present) must be replaced with '**had finished**' to maintain logical sequence and grammatical accuracy.

Therefore, the correct answer is **provided he had finished**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The supervisor did not mind if a worker left early, **provided he had finished** his task for the day.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 'provided he will finish'** – This uses the **Future Tense**, which is incorrect because the narrative is set in the past.
 
• **Option 2: 'provided he is finishing'** – This uses the **Present Continuous Tense**, which implies the action is currently happening and does not fit the past context.
 
• **Option 4: 'No improvement required'** – This is incorrect because the original 'finishes' is in the **Simple Present Tense**, creating a tense clash with the past tense verbs 'did' and 'left'.
</ul

questions.question:
From the given alternatives, choose the correct meaning of the following idiom/phrase.
A political football.

options.text: An argument that suggests the probable effects of a known cause or using general principles to suggest likely effects.
An issue that is the subject of continuous argument or controversy.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **An issue that is the subject of continuous argument or controversy.**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **'A political football'** refers to a topical issue or problem that is constantly debated and used by opposing political parties to gain an advantage over each other, rather than being solved. (एक ऐसा मुद्दा जिस पर राजनीतिक लाभ के लिए निरंतर बहस या विवाद होता हो)
 
 
• **Example: **The debate over **environmental regulations** has become a **political football**, with neither side willing to compromise.
 
 
 
• **'An issue that is the subject of continuous argument or controversy'** perfectly describes the nature of a political football, where the topic remains a point of contention for a long period. (सतत तर्क या विवाद का विषय)
 
 
• **Example: **The **funding for public schools** remained an issue that was the subject of **continuous argument** during the entire election cycle.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'a political football'** is **'an issue that is the subject of continuous argument or controversy'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **An issue that is the subject of continuous argument or controversy.**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **An argument that suggests the probable effects of a known cause **(एक ऐसा तर्क जो ज्ञात कारणों से संभावित प्रभावों का सुझाव देता है): This refers to **a priori reasoning**, where one predicts an outcome based on general principles.
 
 
• **Example:** The economist provided an **a priori argument** that the new tax would eventually lead to lower consumer spending.
 
 
 
• **A signal that something is not working properly **(एक संकेत कि कुछ ठीक से काम नहीं कर रहा है): Often referred to as a **red flag** or a **warning sign**.
 
 
• **Example: **The high turnover rate of employees was a **clear signal** that the company culture was toxic.
 
 
 
• **A puzzle difficult to solve **(एक कठिन पहेली): This refers to a **conundrum** or a **complex enigma** that is hard to figure out.
 
 
• **Example: **How to provide enough energy for the growing population without harming the planet is a **puzzle difficult to solve**.

These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence/passage and find the most logical order of the parts between 1 and 6.

1. Letter writing is a way of sending messages through written words. 

P. Letters can be formal or informal depending on the purpose. 

Q. In the body of the letter, we clearly express our thoughts or requests. 

R. We end the letter with a polite closing line. 

S. A letter usually begins with a greeting to the person we are writing to. 

6. Good letter writing needs clear language, respect, and correct format.
questions.solution:

• **Sentence S is the first sentence** in the arrangement as it describes the beginning of the letter structure: 
• 'A letter usually begins with a **greeting** to the person we are writing to.' 
• **Sentence Q follows** as it describes the next logical step in the letter-writing process, which is the content: 
• 'In the **body of the letter**, we clearly express our thoughts or requests.' 
• **Sentence R is the third sentence** because it explains how the written message is concluded: 
• 'We end the letter with a **polite closing line**.' 
• **Sentence P is the fourth** as it categorizes letters based on their nature (**formal or informal**) before the final summary in sentence 6: 
• 'Letters can be **formal or informal** depending on the purpose.' 
• The correct logical sequence is **SQRP**.
